newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba officials happy with dollar, eye steady rates.
newsitem.headline: Buba officials happy with dollar, eye steady rates.

text.p: Bundesbank officials on Tuesday reemphasised that Germany was still happy with the dollar's current level but hinted a significantly stronger dollar would not be welcome, helping briefly unhinge the currency market.

Central bank council member Ernst Welteke told reporters that the Bundesbank was happy with the dollar's level of around 1.70 marks, stressing that a few pfennings lower or higher were not perceived as a problem. But he added "we cannot welcome a further rise in the dollar."
An incorrect report that Welteke had put a number on the Bundesbank's tolerance for the dollar's level quickly sent the currency nearly one pfennig lower from its 1.73 marks level.

German officials including Bundesbank members as well as finance and economics ministry officials studiously avoid mentioning any specific dollar levels, preferring to speak only in general and often vague terms.
Welteke's spokesman told Reuters that Welteke had definitely not given "any levels at which the Bundesbank might no longer be happy with the dollar and he certainly did not give a four digit level."
A news agency had reported the Bundesbank would be unhappy if the dollar exceeded the 1.7350 mark level.

At the same time Welteke's council colleague Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, president of the state central bank in Berlin and Brandenburg, said the dollar's current levels were still supporting Germany's export driven economy.

Although some independent economists fear Germany might soon import inflation through rising import prices, three council members said fundamental factors still did not indicate a near-term shift in interest rates would be necessary.

Franz-Christoph Zeitler, the president of the state central bank in Bavaria, citing ongoing low inflation rates and efforts to pare back government deficits, said "Based on the fundamental factors I see no reason for a change of direction in interest rates."
Welteke added, "At the moment the Bundesbank is well advised to follow a straight course on interest rates and thereby stabilise the expectations of financial markets."
Nervousness that the Bundesbank might however be forced to end its five year easing cycle and raise rates has increased especially after several other countries decided hiked rates.
The U.K. on Tuesday stunned financial markets by lifting rates to 6.25 percent just weeks after the U.S. fired a similar warning shot at revived inflationary pressures in late March.
Council members were however divided on Germany's chances of meeting the entatch 1995's 756 million mark level.
Lufthansa in mid-April announced that its 1996 operating profit would be just below its pre-tax profit figure of almost 700 million marks.

In a statement issued in response to an article in German business magazine Capital, Lufthansa said that its 1996 figures would not match those seen in 1995 but that losses would be "far below" those alleged in the article.
In the statement released today, Lufthansa said 1996 full year and 1997 first quarter results would be detailed at Wednesday's news conference.
